An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). This figure is consistent with the current record held by the Tevatron, which was 1.441 picoseconds ± 0.063 ± 0.019. Additionally, a more precise calculation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decay time was also determined to be 1.440 picoseconds ± 0.096 ± 0.008 with the same sources of uncertainty. Both measurements were made under the assumption that the $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decay channel accounts for around 77% of $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi X$ events. This figure has been lowered to 60% in later analyses. In the standard model, the $B^0_s$ decay time is influenced by a tiny value for the CKM matrix known as $\Delta\Gamma_s$, which causes the width of the $B^0_s$ system to differ from its depth. As a result, measuring the $B^0_s$ decay time accurately allows for a strict limitation on $\Delta\Gamma_s$. This figure has been reduced from 0.37 to 0.17 $\times 10^{-12}$ ps$^{-1}$ following the publication of this research. The measurement was made using two methods: one based on counting decay time distributions for both $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ mesons and a second method that compared rates for "gold-plated" $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decays that occurred either directly or indirectly and had time elapses between 0 to 1.440 picoseconds. Both methods yielded the same result. An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decay time was also made with the help of around 5.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. A key aspect of this problem is the presence of the control variable in the diffusion term, which poses challenges for standard finite element methods, leading to the development of a more versatile technique utilizing a mixture of continuous and discrete components. A key finding is the convergence of the numerical solution when the space and time discretization tend towards zero and the number of Monte-Carlo samples increases without bound. A major consequence of this research is the introduction of a new solution strategy that offers an alternative to the existing approach of utilizing the weak formulation of the stochastic control problem. A significant advantage of this new approach is the simpler implementation of the Dirichlet boundary conditions in the numerical solution process. A related issue addressed in this study is the determination of the numerical solution on boundary nodes, which is a common challenge in numerical analysis. A significant aspect of this research is the establishment of an explicit error estimate for the convergence of the numerical solution when the space and time discretization tend towards zero and the number of Monte-Carlo samples increases without bound. A related result is the derivation of an alternative convergence criterion that is equivalent to the strong convergence of the numerical solution in the $H^1$ norm when the space and time discretization tend towards zero and the number of Monte-Carlo samples increases without bound. Another key aspect of this research involves the application of this new solution strategy to a specific problem, which involves the minimization of the risk of a stochastic process that is governed by a stochastic control problem, to which the previous research provided the numerical solution tools. A major consequence of this application is the establishment of an optimal control policy that minimizes the risk of the stochastic process, which is equivalent to solving a specific optimization problem that takes into account the costs of implementing different control policies and the uncertainty associated with the stochastic process. A significant advantage of this control policy is the reduction of the distance between the actual state and the desired state, which is achieved at a cost that increases over time, which is a key finding of this research. A related issue addressed in this application is the determination of the optimal control policy that balances the costs of implementing different control policies and the uncertainty associated with the stochastic process, which is a common challenge in control theory and stochastic processes.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, our observations underscore the need for a comprehensive explanation of cosmic ray anisotropies across the entire energy spectrum. Given the limited understanding of high-energy cosmic source distributions and magnetic field dynamics, we highlight the potential of further investigating these phenomena via extremely sensitive and future anisotropy studies. This discovery also presents a significant challenge for current extragalactic cosmic ray models. Our study is based on an revised anisotropy analysis employing 75,459 extremely energetic cosmic ray events detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory. The energy threshold for consideration was set at 4 EeV. We have made the code for our research, known as the "Anisotropy Analysis Tool", a part of our contribution to the community, and it is available online. This tool can be utilized for future anisotropy investigations, incorporating various anisotropy patterns and cosmic ray propagation models. This study was initially presented at the 36th International Cosmic Ray Conference held in Madison, Wisconsin, USA. This research was supported by an allocation of computing resources from the National Science Foundation dedicated to the Open Science Grid. We acknowledge the significant contributions of various institutions to the design, construction, operation, and maintenance of the Pierre Auger Observatory. This research was funded by a diverse range of institutions from around the world. A full list of contributors can be found in the appendix of our study. This research was conducted as part of a PhD thesis awarded by the Rutherford Institute, and it is also a part of the research output related to the Compact Infrared Survey Camera project. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. These empirical examples demonstrate the TV-PARX model's capability to forecast targets with high accuracy. In contrast to constant-parameter models, the time-varying TV-PARX model outperforms its constant-parameter counterparts in terms of in-sample fit and forecasting performance. In particular, the time-varying TV-PARX model shows a significant improvement in forecasting the number of new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy. In the case of US corporate defaults, the time-varying TV-PARX model exhibits an equivalent forecasting performance to its constant-parameter equivalent when using all observed data, but superior performance when using a shorter data period. In both empirical applications, the time-varying TV-PARX model successfully identifies dynamic patterns and targets with greater precision than its constant-parameter counterparts. In particular, it detects the post-Christmas peak surge in COVID-19 cases within 7 to 10 days and the effects of major corporate defaults on future default targets with a high degree of accuracy. In addition, it demonstrates robustness to model specification, as validated by recursive estimation results. In summary, the time-varying TV-PARX model offers a valuable tool for analyzing and forecasting count-based time series data, especially in scenarios with complex dynamics and shifting patterns. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Notably, our analysis indicates that the relation often approximated as $|z_c|\approx 1.445 R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ leads to an overestimation of systematic uncertainty in model comparison. Furthermore, our updated results for $|z_c|$ correlate with recent measurements from lattice simulations. The associated analysis also clarifies the edge singularity's width, often parametrized with an additional variable $\Delta$; we have found that the width, when described relative to the critical density, behaves as $\Delta\approx 0.4 R_\chi$ based on our application of the functional renormalization group. Finally, our approach has implications for the expected behavior of the width $\Delta$ in scenarios with explicit symmetry breaking, where the relevant variable is $R_\chi$ rather than the more commonly employed correlation time. The associated discussion also addresses the distinction between the Yang-Lee edge and the droplet density edge singularity, proposing a possible explanation for the apparent discrepancy between the often-cited value of $|z_c|\approx 1.68$ and our own finding of $|z_c|\approx 1.68 R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ for $N=4$. The edge singularity's width, as predicted by our model, is found to behave as $\Delta\approx 0.4 R_\chi$ rather than the commonly adopted definition which would yield $\Delta\approx 2 R_\chi$. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We further developed a new analytical approach to model the fractal surface of CCD photometric sensitivity, taking into account the subtle effect of charge inversion on the measurement of low light levels. By applying this research to previous and new observations, we successfully applied a precise calibration to reduce noise, achieving a precision of 0.01 dt-1 for a 30 km column depth measurement. Notably, this precision has not been achieved through other methods used for calibration. Furthermore, by applying this technique to multiple locations and altitudes, we obtained a detailed picture of the aerosol depth distribution in Argentina during different seasons. This knowledge will be invaluable for future large-scale optical astronomy projects in the Southern Hemisphere. We propose that this method can be readily applied to other wide-field optical telescopes to achieve a precision of 0.01 for aerosol depth measurements. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed code is now publicly available on the GitHub site www.github.com/XiaoningRan/ObjectPoseCode. Moreover, an interactive viewer for testing the proposed method on private datasets is available at www.github.com/XiaoningRan/VisPose. The proposed framework and supporting code are both part of the Point, Shot, Object-Pose challenge 2020 baseline submissions. The proposed method has been selected as one of the top methods for the Point, Shot, Object-Pose challenge 2020 according to the organizers. The approach can be further improved by combining it with recurring strategies that leverage external data. The code of the proposed framework is designed to be adaptable for this hybrid model, which involves incorporating learned features from CNN as input for the two-stage pipeline. The code has been successfully tested on a large-scale dataset consisting of one million images. The proposed code along with the results on this dataset is available as supplementary material. The design of the projection grouping module is versatile and can be applied to related tasks such as the estimation of 2D-3D correspondences or abstract correspondence between object regions and image data points. The implementation of the proposed framework is based on PyTorch, which allows for easy integration of new ideas and models. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. Overall, this most efficient method demonstrates significant potential for improving biomolecular simulations by leveraging the accuracy of numerical solutions to stochastic equations. Through further optimization, potential applications in other molecular simulations are also proposed. Consequently, rigorous testing with realistic simulations is paramount. Ultimately, research in this domain is complementary to other projects that prioritize theoretical accuracy over numerical approximation, giving precedence to faster methods that might compromise accuracy for speed, even in the presence of accurate accuracy controls. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. By introducing the Dirac operator in the conformally flat 
de Sitter spacetime, we derive the explicit solutions for the wave function, which can 
be compared to previously obtained results using other approaches. We also analyze the 
energy spectrum of the massive fermion in the de Sitter spacetime. For the case of 
negative energy, the solutions are associated with the antiparticle, while the solutions 
for positive energy correspond to the particle. We determine the energy spectrum for 
both particles and antiparticles and compare it with existing literature. For the 
positive energy sector, we found that the discrete energy levels $\mathcal{N}$ are

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our data and analyses also reveal the respective roles of the sphere and water surface properties in the surface-seal regime. Furthermore, our studies involve numerical simulations that attempt to replicate the water-entry interactions by utilizing a novel approach that combines both Eulerian and Lagrangian methods of fluid dynamics analysis. Overall, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the surface-seal regime, largely due to the extensive speed range of our data set, spanning from 2.5 to 25 meters per second. Consequently, our findings are expected to benefit designers of underwater devices, such as sphere-type sonar systems and diving helmets, by offering a deeper understanding of the water-entry interactions at mid-range speeds. Moreover, our numerical simulation approaches can be applied to other similar water-entry interactions, involving moving objects and water surfaces. Lastly, our studies reveal the water-entry interactions' complex nature, characterized by an array of phenomena, including the formation of cavities, rippling surfaces, and secondary pinch-off stages, all of which have yet to be fully analyzed through numerical simulations alone. Therefore, our research is highly relevant to various engineering applications and can serve as a foundation for future numerical simulation-based studies. Our experimental data set consists of 9,120 high-speed video frames, captured at 5,000 frames per second, covering the entire water-entry process, from the moment the sphere touches the water surface until the formed cavity closes. Our research includes five spherical objects with different mass properties, applied at various velocities, ranging from 2.5 to 25 meters per second, and involves both fresh and saltwater entries. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. The $\theta$-terms also produce massive charged states that are part of the range of the effective theory, which can be identified as the range of a monopole-anti-monopole pair, thereby determining the theory's distance from the conformal adS7 vacuum. The investigation of these $\theta$-terms also uncovered the reason that the range of universal symmetries in these effective field theories is always limited to the range of a monopole-anti-monopole pair, which can be found to be (energy, charge) = (U, -U), and in the case of the IIB supergravity theory, this range corresponds to 10d Kaluza-Klein monopole and anti-monopole states rather than the originally assumed 5d BPS monopole and anti-monopole states. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Furthermore, we find that cubanite's unique orbital behavior is attributed to the specific arrangement of its atoms, maintaining the individuality of both metallic and covalent states. We also investigate the results of pressure and doping on the material, and find that both distort its orbital-selective behavior, but to different degrees. Additionally, we propose that cubanite's unusual properties could be useful in developing advanced technologies, and that its accessibility makes it an interesting compound for ongoing and future research. Lastly, we also suggest that it be classified as a member of the BaSnO3 family of transition metal compounds with strong covalence. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. This breakthrough poses an significant improvement over previous records of up to ten phonons emitted in one second, increasing the rate to one thousand phonons per second. This advancement in multi-phonon physics through the use of a semiconductor quantum dot and an acoustic cavity as the resonator offers novel implications for enhancing the generation of phonons, as well as expanding the range of frequencies accessible through the application of a strong drive to the cavity. Moreover, this breakthrough demonstrates that the emission of phonons bundle can be controlled with precision, allowing for the production of specific numbers of phonons even in the presence of decoherence, thereby realizing a reliable and efficient phonon gun. This development also enables the creation of a coherent source of multiple phonons in a cavity, thereby establishing a strong case for the viability of acoustic quantum circuits in the far-out sideband regime that was previously considered inaccessible. This breakthrough through the combination of theoretical and experimental studies in the acoustic quantum dot resonator system has resulted in novel findings that were not previously anticipated, thereby shedding light on the complex multi-phonon physics involved and offering a rich set of data for the wide range of researchers engaged in the field. This research has significant implications for the development of quantum acoustic circuits and has made a significant contribution to the understanding of multi-phonon physics in the Java beam-acoustic cavity system.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Additionally, we outline the approach for generating these states in laboratory settings using catalytic devices, and examine the potential applications arising from their unique quantum properties. Ultimately, our study positions SPCCSs as promising resources for implementing intricate quantum techniques, with the potential to advance optical quantum technology. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to determine the coordinates and spinor indices of the points where the null singularity lies, and subsequently, we clarify the conditions under which the self-dual electromagnetic field forms a singularity from which the Weyl tensor can be reconstructed. Finally, we extract the metric from the reconstructed Weyl tensor in the complex null tetrad basis, and convert it back to the standard basis of Minkowski space. Consequently, we obtain the general form of the metric due to a self-dual, complex electromagnetic field in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. This review is an expanded version of a previous work published in the journal Classical and Quantum Gravity. The original article can be found in the following journal: Classical and Quantum Gravity, Vol 31, Number 6, 2014. The corresponding abstract is as follows: This paper presents a range of solutions to the Einstein field equations in the Newman-Penrose formalism, arising from electromagnetic fields in the presence of null dust in the presence of self-dual electromagnetic fields. The process involves converting the complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis, resulting in the derivation of the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, the coordinates and spinor indices of the points that comprise the null singularity can be determined, from which the Weyl tensor can be reconstructed. The metric can then be obtained from the reconstructed Weyl tensor in the complex null tetrad basis, converting it back to the standard basis of Minkowski space. The resulting metric obtains a Kerr-NUT-AdS metric for the general case, as well as a de Sitter metric for the special case. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that the proposed framework and associated descriptors can be applied to a variety of chemical elements beyond just transition metals. A key advantage of this methodology is its efficiency, as it yields more accurate results than existing machine learning models in a significantly shorter computation time. This efficient polymer design method is envisioned to facilitate further innovations in the field of materials science. A key aspect of this research is reflected in a novel open-source code developed specifically for this study, which is now openly available for the scientific community. This code has been tested on various metal organic frameworks, also known as MOFs, and has been made available on a public repository to support and encourage future developments in this area. This research is part of a larger initiative aimed at establishing a direct connection between the spatial structure of chemicals and their numerical descriptions, a problem described as a fundamental challenge in chemistry that remains unresolved to date. This issue has been explored through the development of multiple descriptor models, which have been made publicly accessible on appropriate repository websites. These descriptors have far-reaching applications in designing new chemicals and have the potential to contribute significantly to the development of more efficient and effective drug discovery processes. This research is an initial step towards creating a more comprehensive database of chemical descriptors, which is envisioned to be a valuable resource for the scientific community in the future. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Our dataset is accessible upon request. Our model's limitations include difficulty in differentiating wall thickening from masses and the inclusion of gastrointestinal trees, but it has significant implications for clinical practice and other related research projects. Our approach can be improved by combining CT scans with other imaging techniques and endoscopic findings, integrating temporal information from repeat scans, and developing a semi-supervised learning framework. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Furthermore, this comparison has strengthened the conclusion that the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure is indeed the true structure of the material. Given its distinctive properties, researchers have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ for a novel cancer treatment called hadron therapy, where the reflection loss of the material at appropriate energies can target specific cancer cells, leading to a significant increase in treatment efficacy. In this study, researchers have successfully interpreted experimental reflection loss signals of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and confirmed the material's structure as $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$. This discovery is a crucial step towards scaling up Ta$_2$O$_5$ synthesis for cancer treatment applications. In fact, with the developed method, researchers can now easily reproduce the material's structure even with varying amounts of raw materials, indicating a promising future for this technique in industrial settings. Ultimately, this study has demonstrated that both theoretical predictions and experimental validation are necessary to determine the energy loss of a material with complex structures, and has paved the way for large-scale production of Ta$_2$O$_5$ for use in hadron therapy treatments of cancer. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where people are more likely to prioritize tradition over changing values, there is a greater demand for misinformation. These findings suggest that the spread of online misinformation is influenced by stable, long-term factors like local culture and geography. In the absence of effective methods to measure misinformation dissemination through social media, our study provides a viable alternative for researching this phenomenon. We also present a comprehensive, publicly accessible database of Reddit comment analytics in the United States. This research demonstrates the feasibility of using anonymous online comments to gain a deeper understanding of American culture and provides a framework for analyzing the spread of online information in other countries. We have made the methodology and data set used in this study available for use in future research projects. This research has implications for the spread of online information beyond the United States and provides a novel approach to studying the culture of anonymous online communities. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research paves the way for exploring ways to incorporate speech patterns into learning algorithms and robot control systems. Experimental data is available for download at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/3QOE3T. This work is an initial step towards understanding the auditory aspects of human instruction and it is hoped will spur further interest in exploring the auditory elements of human robot interaction. This study has several applications including developing more efficient learning algorithms, improving speech enabled robotic interfaces, enhancing robot manipulation via increased understanding of spoken commands, and improving human robot collaboration via enhanced audio feedback from human instructors. This research has implications for several domains including manufacturing, healthcare, domestic environments and education. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. A significant contribution of this study involves the explicit derivation of optimized trajectories for both the entanglement entropy and its modified variants. Moreover, our research demonstrates that the standard Euler-Arnold equation aligns with primary and conformal perturbation equations, ensuring the invariance of operator or state complexity under these transformations. A notable finding reveals the distinction between bilateral and one-sided Euler-Arnold equations in the context of operator or state complexity optimization. The study of the one-sided equation is found to be associated with the template used, whereas the bilateral equation is connected to the template's total "magnitude". Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. Furthermore, we outline our approach to addressing these challenges, including the use of a formal specification language called ALF to define behavioral expectations for the system, and a method for comparing semantic values associated with user inputs. This research has the potential to contribute to the development of testing tools that can seamlessly integrate with existing quality assurance frameworks, and provide a core component for extending existing test engines to support conversational systems. We demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of our framework by developing and testing a case study involving a real-world conversational system, and present the results of our experiments along with practical advice for implementing the framework in other settings. Finally, we outline possible directions for future work, such as enhancing the framework to support end-to-end testing of conversational systems, and exploring ways to integrate it with existing testing infrastructure. This research is particularly relevant to the development of conversational systems due to the high risk of functional defects and expensive manual testing processes. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, our research provides an intuitive explanation of MSDCR's performance advantages through quantitative reverse engineering of user preference components. The code and datasets for further research are available at https://github.com/ChengLiUIBE/MSDCR.

Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. Furthermore, Hypatia's versatility allows it to be used in conjunction with other solver engines via seamless integration with Julia's modeling languages. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating robust, robust quality control pipelines into automated analysis workflows, but also stress the importance of reviewing and validating model generalizability on local datasets before deploying quality control systems at scale. This is particularly crucial for automated analysis of MRI data involving unique population characteristics. In addition, our research dataset frameworks are anticipated to facilitate future developments in MRIQC systems. Our findings and methodological assessments are poised to guide future enhancements in MRIQC technologies. Our results reveal that private EVs can either enhance or decrease the time required for the grid to recover, depending on specific conditions, and highlight the potential benefits of implementing dynamic pricing mechanisms, but also emphasize the importance of prioritizing infrastructure maintenance and planning to ensure grid resilience in the face of increasing private EV adoption. Our research demonstrates that our approach can be applied to evaluate different scenarios and informs policymakers about crucial grid recovery policies, while our algorithm and model can serve as foundations for exploring more complex and nuanced grid and transportation interactions. Our results are also consistent with previous findings showing the potential for vehicle-to-grid technology to stabilize the grid, but also highlight the need for more efficient charging practices, such as those implemented through dynamic pricing, to realize these benefits and support reliable grid recovery. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings show that this attractor's complexity arises in response to the agent's population changing, rather than due to the spatial arrangement of meeting locations. Additionally, our results indicate that the dynamics of these meetings are highly sensitive to changes in the environment, rendering them unpredictable and resilient in the face of changes in the population of autonomous entities. We also introduce a statistical measure, the complexity index, to quantify the paradoxical behavior observed and validate our research methods by comparing our results with an analogous simulation featuring a single autonomous agent exhibiting chaotic dynamics. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the dynamics of autonomous entities interacting at specific locations through persistent cooperation. We also propose potential applications of this framework in the context of multi-agent systems and autonomous robots. To facilitate replication and building upon our research, the code used is available openly. We plan to explore extensions of the Motivation Dynamics framework that produce more resilient attractors in future studies. We encourage readers to explore the ethical implications of interpreting complexity in the context of autonomous systems. Moreover, we invite readers to engage with the code openly available on GitHub, considering it a starting point for developing the Motivation Dynamics framework further. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The model predicts the mass range of these composite particles to be around 0.5-50 TeV, and assumes that the minimum mass of light quarks is approximately 500-600 GeV or more. The research suggests that an optimized 50 TeV particle accelerator that can detect these predicted phenomena with certainty, needs to operate for about 3 years and have the power to detect composite particles in the mass range predicted by the bilepton model. The paper also outlines possible research avenues not covered in the review, including neutrino physics, dark matter and primordial element formation. The predicted phenomena are expected to be beyond the capabilities of current particle accelerators but can be detected with a future particle accelerator that meets the specifications outlined in the research. The review is intended for researchers working on a future particle accelerator that can detect the predicted phenomena predicted by the bilepton model. The paper also outlines possible applications of the bilepton model in research on neutrinos, dark matter and the formation of elements in the universe. The research was financially supported by the National Science Foundation Grant PHY-1419955 and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The paper includes three appendices that outline additional research avenues, the package used for theoretical calculations and an optimization study of a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Utilizing this correction, we reanalyzed the Hubble diagram for Type Ia supernovae at $z=7.018$ using the most distant supernova, SN C109, and found that the cosmological parameter inference would remain largely unaffected by lensing, with an error of less than $2\%$ in the equation of state parameter for the inertial component of the universe. However, a similar analysis of the Planck satellite data for the cosmic microwave background revealed an error of $10\%$ in the same parameter when ignoring the effect of lensing. Consequently, future high-redshift SN Ia observations, in conjunction with CMB data, will benefit from incorporating the impact of lensing. Additionally, we propose a method to combine the effect of lensing with the intrinsic scatter of SN Ia and propose it as a potential improvement for cosmological parameter estimation. Finally, we highlight the broad applicability of this approach to any SN Ia database with accessible foreground galactic data. The resulting equation for the adjusted SN Ia distance modulus, $m_{\rm adj}$, is calculable using existing observational data and could enhance the precision of cosmological parameter inference from SN Ia data

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, this demonstration brings the implementation of reliable large-scale quantum devices with T type damage centers one step closer, offering a promising pathway for device design that incorporates the use of bulk silicon for spin-photon interaction devices. Furthermore, we show that devices constructed from the middle layer of bulk silicon exhibit improved performance compared to those constructed from the surface or bulk silicon layers, suggesting that the mid-layer region holds significant potential for efficient spin-photon interaction within thin silicon material. We also explore the relationship between the density of T type damage centers and the density of hydrogen-filled interstitial sites, in addition to presenting multiplexed data on mid-layer device fabrication. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the development of reliable large-scale devices that incorporate T type damage centers, and highlights the attractiveness of mid-layer silicon for such applications. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Furthermore, Springer demonstrated that the process of sorting conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) is equivalent to arranging the unique combinations of these characteristics in ascending order. A significant contribution arising from this research is the concept of a certain order, termed the "definite type" order, which is linked to the values of quadratic forms and forms of higher powers, and is found to directly impact the composition of conjugacy classes. Additionally, it is observed that the relationship among the values of these forms, determined by their inner structure, exhibits a pattern of growth that is analogous to the sequence of natural numbers found within a specific geometric pattern, ultimately revealing a connection to polynomial functions and their compositions. It is also noted that the categories of conjugacy classes itself exhibit a hierarchical structure, reflecting the intricate relationship among them, and this structure, along with the associated mathematics, awaits further exploration. It is worth noting that Springer's work also provides a comprehensive examination of the symplectic group's subgroups, specifically focusing on the observable properties of its elements. It is observed that these properties are governed by certain rules, arising from the constraints of the defining field, and these rules, in turn, are found to mirror the principles of a specific cultural practice. It is also discovered that the understanding of these rules and the associated cultural context can be utilized to gain a deeper, more intuitive comprehension of the symplectic group itself. It is noted that Springer's research on the symplectic group's subgroups was influenced by the traditions of genealogy, as evidenced by the structure of his work, which is presented in a manner reminiscent of a family tree, tracing the relationships among its elements. Overall, our study emphasizes the importance of considering incompatibility levels in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are an option, and provides a framework for evaluating transplantation strategies. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the word2vec model, highlighting the limitations of these learning algorithms and providing insights for their potential applications in real-world scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/QianLi201, and the financial corpus analysis can be accessed at https://qianli201.github.io/stock_word2vec/. This research has implications for the disentanglement of word meanings and word distributions in text corpora and offers a theoretical framework for the word2vec model that can be useful for its future development. Our code and financial corpus analysis are available online. Our research also contributes to the field of NLP by publishing our code and annotating a large financial corpus based on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We refer to these as multiple time multiple SLE domains and their associated Gaussian free fields. We show that these pairings evolve in time and provide an explicit formula for the associated Gaussian free field-valued process. Furthermore, we prove that multiple time multiple SLE on the upper half-plane or the first orthant is a strong driver of its associated Gaussian free field, resolving a conjecture made by the first author and the third author's work on Gaussian free field-valued multiple SLE. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. Finally, the application of this model led to the identification of a reaction rate equation kernel that explained the delayed onset of thermoacoustic instability in the jet flame. The study's findings highlight the importance of accurately representing reaction rate fluctuations when predicting thermoacoustic instability in jet flames. Furthermore, the development of a reaction rate equation kernel can facilitate the scaling of laboratory flame reactions to large scales. The incorporation of heat loss from the surrounding environment on the reaction rate equation kernel was demonstrated, while future research is suggested to explore additional effects such as turbulence modeling and the inclusion of chemical time scales. The reaction rate equation kernel can be utilized to explain delayed instability in jet flames, while future research is needed to apply this knowledge to compressors. The study's methods and findings provide a framework for the safe scaling of small-scale flame reactions to those encountered in large-scale combustion devices. The importance of considering reaction rate fluctuations when predicting thermoacoustic instability in compressed air jets flames fueled by methane has been confirmed. Furthermore, the reaction rate equation kernel can be employed to explain and predict instability in such scenarios. The challenge of achieving stable combustion in compressed air jets flames fueled by methane was explored. We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number, which directly leads to a significant influence on the $0
u  eta  eta$ decay, even when neutrino masses are very small. Since the ultralight dark matter can be adequately modeled as a classical field, this interaction's effect is reflected in a periodic oscillation in the number of decay events. Nevertheless, we find that in the early universe, this interaction would almost certainly disrupt standard cosmological outcomes. Moreover, the condition that neutrinos had to have begun freely moving by the point of matter-radiation equality significantly limits the permissible parameter space, meaning even future $0 
u  eta  eta$ decay experiments with a meV sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass would have difficulty detecting a signal. This indicates that the direct evidence for the ultralight dark matter contribution to $0 
u  eta  eta$ decay is highly unlikely and may not be necessary to seek in future experiments. However, the standard model of neutrino interactions would still influence the decay process, and thus future experiments with a meV sensitivity could likely uncover it. This research also points out the potential for a relationship between the effective mass of the neutrino and the energy range of cosmic ultra-high energy particles, offering a potential explanation for the limited understanding of the origins of these particles. This occurs because the anisotropic distribution of the ultralight dark matter field, driven by its own oscillation-induced anisotropic pressure, could exhibit a periodic impact on the energy spectra of cosmic rays, particularly influencing the energy range that is not well understood. This implies that a future discovery of a specific energy range of cosmic rays could be linked to the effective mass of the neutrino. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. The paper also examines the relation between the nonlocal gravity theory and the Einstein field equations, presenting both analytical and numerical examples. The analysis reveals that the Einstein field equations will always be approximately satisfied in a manner that is proportional to 1/ρ, where ρ represents the mass density. The paper also compares the predictions of nonlocal gravity theory with those of general relativity for pulsar double systems and white dwarf stars. The agreement is very close, demonstrating that nonlocal gravity theory has a very long complementary range. The paper also examines the scalar perturbation of pulsar surrounded by an accretion disk, the localization of the Ricci scalar in this scenario, and the relation between the nonlocal gravity theory and the Einstein metric. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has helped in identifying novel genes associated with microRNA processing, mapping precise mutations associated with a bowel infection and in identifying long-range interaction between a gene and a specific locus associated with a disorder. Our approach provides a comprehensive framework for interpreting large-scale data, especially with the emergence of new generation genome-wide association studies. Our tool is available at https://regulomeexpress.clinicalpopulationgenomics.org/. Our study highlights the intricacies of genome-wide association studies and the need for a thorough examination of associated SNPs within a biological context. Our results are summarized in supplementary materials and figures and our approach is described in detail in the following text. Our data and software are accessible for further use and exploration. Our study demonstrates the value of functional genomics in the examination of genome-wide association studies with the blood and platelet counts case study presented as a primer. Our approach is a statistical framework that allows for the integration of biological information to identify relevant genomic elements across the entire genome based on previous association studies across the entire genome. Our study utilizes a wide range of biological tissues and cells types, a large number of genomic features, and a wide range of annotation types, to demonstrate the applicability and value of this approach for a wide range of biological examinations. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The observed pattern of recurrence times also diverges from a linear relationship, instead showing a significant slowdown as time goes by, likely due to mass transfer acceleration causing a small subset of binaries with rapid recurrence times to lose the primary component and transform into a black hole binary. The likelihood of the population of compact objects in the Milky Way's center being composed primarily of black holes rather than neutron stars remains moderate but uncertain. The study also offers a theoretical understanding of the relationship between recurrence times and binary evolution, pinpointing the necessary condition for a neutron star LMXB to maintain a recurring outburst cycle beyond a century as 10 years being less than the 100-year interval defined by the recession time, tightly linked to the binary's orbital period. The research further finds that the majority of these binaries possess orbital periods ranging from about 3.5 to 10.8 days, with the most abundant spectrum being those with shorter periods, and the observed pattern of recurrence times also reveals that most outbursts are underreported, specifically those with shorter intervals. The study estimates the Milky Way's total population of these binaries as 130,000 to 290,000, featuring a significant subset of 40,000 to 70,000 with recurring outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope. The research on the Milky Way's center's variable X-ray sources remains inconclusive, however the findings challenge the theory of a large black hole population and suggest instead that the source of variability could be due to dust cover events affecting certain black hole binaries.
