The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In both cases, we found that, despite rapid spin causing mass loss and size reduction, the conditions for sustainable hydrogen burning remained largely unchanged. This is in contrast to previous studies suggesting that more spin leads to a shift in the conditions necessary for hydrogen burning. The simulations also demonstrated that rotating low-mass stars tend to maintain a specific minimum mass (approximately 0.014 solar masses) before they cease hydrogen burning and the conditions for this process become more restrictive. This research suggests that the minimum mass required for sustainable hydrogen burning in low-mass stars is primarily determined by internal forces, rather than external forces such as gravity from a companion star. This is particularly relevant to the study of sub-stellar objects formed through binary interactions. This can lead to a wider range of possible masses for which we should be searching in binary star interactions, specifically those with initial mass ratios between approximately 0.05 to 0.25. This could result in the formation of low-mass stars with conditions suitable for sustainable hydrogen burning, with minimum masses currently not accounted for in binary star interactions. This research also predicts possible features of these low-mass stars, including their composition, size, and luminosity, as well as the possible detection methods for identifying them. These features suggest that these stars could be found in the habitability zones of binary star systems, and might be more likely to be found in regions of the galaxy with higher binary star interactions, such as the Carina region. This could lead to the possibility of finding life on very low-mass stars that have the capability for sustainable nuclear reactions, and that are located in regions with the right conditions to support life.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In addition, algorithms have been developed to find the minimum number of nodes needed to break in order to achieve an edge-free representation, and to map large-scale bipartite graphs with minimal node breakages, building upon established techniques for planarity testing, flattening, and node splitting. A sample implementation of these methods has been tested on real-world datasets, demonstrating feasible performance even with sizeable input data. The developed approach has implications for understanding and breaking the edge crossings in other types of graphs, including those that are not bipartite. A natural extension of this research could involve the further modification of graph visualizations to enhance their clarity, perhaps by splitting nodes that belong to the same group of objects. In this case, a more sophisticated approach has been proposed, involving the intersection of multiple graphs with the same set of objects, and the mapping of an edge-free supergraph that encompasses all object connections. A sample application of this approach has been tested on a real-world dataset consisting of 500 objects and 10,000 edges, resulting in an edge-free supergraph with 20 nodes that retains key properties of the original graphs. The development of more efficient algorithms to map large-scale supergraphs remains an area of future research. A demonstration of this approach has been made available online. The underlying methods have been made publicly available through an online platform. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. Ultimately, our approach has been demonstrated to result in notable improvements in thuster-assisted gait performance when compared to thruster-only control methods. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. In addition, the authors established that the ring of integers from the $p$-adic field $\mathbb{Q}_p$ cannot be effectively determined with the parameter $t$. This specific result was previously established by Cohen-Guillrayson-Swan in 1980. The associated fields in these results are distinct from the power series fields mentioned earlier. The final section of the paper presents an hypothetical direction for possible future development. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. It has been demonstrated that this method converges to the cooperative equilibrium rapidly. Finally, simulations showed that learning through observation of others along with local experience also enables convergence to the cooperative equilibrium. We also found that learning through observation of others reduces the time it takes to reach the cooperative equilibrium significantly. It has been shown that learning through observation of others leads to a faster convergence to the cooperative equilibrium than learning through local experience alone in scenarios with both small and large variations in task difficulties. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. EFT-based inspiral predictions demonstrate that this design accurately tracks the inspiral phases of binary neutron star mergers. Additionally, this design can detect the characteristic sloshing oscillation modes generated by these mergers, adding a new source of relevant data. Despite the advantages of this design, the sensitivity to end mirror misalignment imposes reasonable alignment requirements on future detector configurations. A proposed intermediate design, building on current LIGO technology, is also presented, along with the code used to calculate the response of the new design. This new design offers a promising future for detecting gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers, particularly in the high-frequency range. To facilitate further research, the code used for calculations has been made publicly available. Although the sloshing Sagnac interferometer design excels in the high-frequency range, it also demonstrates improved sensitivity in the low-frequency range, specifically in the 20-30 Hz band. However, due to fundamental limitations, it is not the most sensitive design in this range. A key aspect of this research is the development of an efficient approach to calculating the response of complex power recycling systems using the modified ray tracing method, in addition to the novel design itself. In the study, the research code was also optimized to facilitate the efficient calculation of detector responses for various phenomena, including those generated by binary neutron star mergers during the inspiral, sloshing oscillation modes during merger and ringdown, and stochastic gravitational waves emitted by neutron stars. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. We found that this gate design yields minimal loss of frequency robustness as the number of ions increases, making it a suitable option for practical quantum computers. Additionally, this design exhibits an entropy growth rate that is roughly half of the total entropy generations from both quadratic drifts in laser frequency and ion motion, demonstrating its ability to efficiently compensate for slight variations in the conditions of individual ions. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves competitive results with respect to current state-of-the-art methods on the large-scale datasets AFLW3000-3D and REFA. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

In an inflationary model, with a specific type of $\alpha$-attractor potential, we examine the behavior in the high-$k$ regime, where cosmological perturbations exhibit excessive growth and negative values of the Bardeen potential. This regime facilitates the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. Our results reveal the formation of PBHs over the $k$ range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, with corresponding mass ranges and properties. These predictions align with forecasts from LISA and other gravitational wave detectors, with a significant overlap in the $f_\mathrm{PBH}$ estimates. Our data further suggest that the astrophysical gap in black hole mass distributions could result from PBHs formed during the inflationary period. Our study predicts specific mass distributions for PBHs, which would result from different inflationary perturbation scales, with the possibility of linking them to the observed astrophysical gap. Our model predicts a solid relation between the number density of PBHs and their mass, with a distinct power-law index (-1.86) that is determined by the inflationary potential only, in addition to an overall number that is influenced by the inflationary scale and other parameters. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the inherent challenges in altering a unit's risk tolerance, our recommendation is to focus on developing risk-affordable storage technology to ensure these systems operate in the best interest of their owners, even if it means forgoing some potential earnings. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. Moreover, both the magnitude of the resistance and the number of oscillations demonstrated a strong correlation with the magnitude of the magnetic field applied, and a specific resistance value was obtained for zero-magnetic-field conditions. This result is particularly significant as it indicates that transport properties of HgTe quantum wells can be understood through a simple, universal parameterization. Additionally, a parameter that defines the width of the heavy-hole reservoir shows a linear relationship with the applied magnetic field, and a parameter that characterizes the edge state shows a non-linear relationship with the applied magnetic field, with a more pronounced non-linearity at zero-magnetic-field conditions. Our research reveals that despite the mesoscopic nature of the samples examined, the energy gap and edge state remain robust, and the transport behavior can be universally described across various sample sizes. This means that accurate modeling of the transport properties of these samples relies heavily on incorporating a magnetic field that takes into account both the external applied and internal field generated by the neutral point. Our study also highlights the potential of using HgTe quantum wells as an ideal material for studying the behavior of edge states in mesoscopic systems. This is further supported by the robustness of these edge states across various sample sizes and magnetic field conditions, and the presence of a wide reservoir of carrier holes that can be controlled through the application of a magnetic field. This makes HgTe quantum wells a highly suitable material for investigating the interaction between edge states and a reservoir of carrier holes. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Moreover, our approach can be easily expanded to account for various TDD scheduling modes and various types of cellular infrastructure. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of dynamic TDD scheduling in challenging cellular settings.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, our proposed system demonstrates comparable performance to models trained on larger datasets but with a significant reduction in computational requirements. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the feasibility of enhancing machine learning through reliable sampling that is environmentally friendly and requires minimal additional data. We have made the code and datasets associated with this research available for public use.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the measurement was used to estimate the total quark-gluon plasma jet density in proton-lead collisions at this energy level, and the fraction of forward-scattered particles contributing to top quark production was found to be 3.6 inverse nanobarns with a 0.9-inverse nanobarn range. These results demonstrate the capability of the CMS experiment to study heavy quark production in heavy ion collisions and provide insights for future studies. The research has been accepted for publication in the European Physical Journal C and is currently available online. The data and analysis utilized in this study were previously used in a report published in Journal of High Energy Physics, volume 2022, issue 4. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Nonetheless, due to the fragmented nature of value filling in Spider, a larger scale dataset is necessary for a more comprehensive evaluation. Nonetheless, our proposed approach has the potential to be extended to other SQL datasets with embedded value information, providing a promising foundation for future research. Our code and models are available for public use at https://github.com/zhong-jianyi/Zero-Shot-SQL.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. Additionally, we demonstrated that this approach can be combined with conventional Bogoliubov methods to solve complex problems involving interfaces and shocks within interacting Bose gases. Ultimately, this work paves the way for further development of stochastic hydrodynamic theories in the context of interacting Bose gases. In order to advance these developments, we suggest potential paths forward, such as exploring interfaces and absorbing boundaries, and providing numerical implementations for solving these problems efficiently. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Experimental findings confirm our proposed approach yields superior results than conventional methods, as measured by model performance and parameter efficacy. The code and data for our experiments are available at https://github.com/zuoyuShi/jkfcv. The main advantage of our proposed approach involves the increased versatility of models trained using j-k fold CV, as evidenced by our experiments conducted using transfer learning, which showed a significant improvement of 2.5% in accuracy after training on a small dataset, alongside a decrease of 20% in parameter numbers. The associated reduction in model size, coupled with the enhanced generalizability, makes the j-k fold CV approach particularly suitable for scenarios involving resource constraints. The approach also offers a key contribution to the development of more reliable and more efficient deep learning models. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Overall, this work reveals the intricate relationships between friction, anisotropy, and shear and provides a robust platform for extrapolating experimental data and guiding simulations of this complex multiphase system. Nonetheless, the inherent difficulties of shearing small groups of particles necessitate the development of future models that can capture the dynamics of this transition with precision. Through a dimensional analysis that leverages fundamental principles and empirical knowledge, researchers have derived a universal expression that connects the stress required to initiate the shear thickening transition with the characteristics of the particles and the fluid they are suspended in. Ultimately, this approach has been applied to the study of silica spheres in glycerol, correcting the existing literature on this subject, and the resulting data points have been made available for open access. The universal nature of the variable that defines the distance from shear jamming to the point of failure has enabled researchers to develop a theoretical framework that explains the characteristics of the stress-volume fraction curve observed in these experiments. The successful application of this approach to a system that exhibits nonlinear behavior through time, involving periodic fluctuations in stress and volume fraction, has been demonstrated. The robustness of this method has been evaluated by integrating the results of experiments conducted at different scales and speeds, and the underlying physics governing the behavior of these multiphase systems has been revealed. The discovery of a universal state variable that governs the behavior of dense mixtures during the shear thickening transition suggests that these systems belong to the same universality class as equilibrium systems that exhibit nonlinear behavior, such as phase transitions in materials

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the proposed method is shown to be viable for both explicit and implicit time-stepping methods, and its effectiveness is illustrated through numerical experiments presented in this work. The results show that by combining the modified flexible generalised minimum residual iteration with the spectral element method, and employing an implicit time-stepping scheme, the proposed method successfully preserves both the property of conservation and the monodissipativity of the numerical solution, even for large time-step sizes. The efficiency and accuracy of this method are validated in the solution of two complex time-dependent PDE systems. The proposed method presents a feasible and efficient strategy for developing time-stepping schemes that enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates the potential to efficiently solve a wide range of PDE systems by preserving both physical properties and stability. The associated software is available for public use and can be downloaded from the corresponding website. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. Furthermore, we present a straightforward approach to incorporate external information, such as intraoperative contrast agent mapping, into the registration process. The resulting navigation data can be utilized for further analytical purposes, such as identifying likely tumor spreads or evaluating surgery outcomes based on postoperative data. The development of an efficient non-rigid registration algorithm for soft-tissue navigation in laparoscopic liver surgery makes the approach feasible for real-time application. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We hope this benchmark and our contributions will facilitate the development of more efficient and accurate self-supervised scene flow estimation models. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, the proposed WRI and ESI methods demonstrate the feasibility of these techniques with real-data examples and the need for further research into challenges related to the large storage needs of the methods.  In particular, the challenge becomes more pronounced with time-domain implementations than with frequency-domain ones.  In the frequency-domain case, successful applications of these methods are possible with relatively small model size projections of about 23 million points or less.  Conversely, time-domain implementations with the same method failed to converge for the same challenge, despite successfully completing the iteration with a much larger storage capacity of about 1 billion points.  Thus, although both frequency and time-domain implementations are viable, the time-domain version is more challenging and more sensitive to the required storage capacity than the frequency-domain version.  In the end, the proposed methods demonstrate the potential of these non-physical source techniques to converge the challenging high-frequency data sets, but also highlight the need for the community to address the significant storage requirements with possible workaround strategies. shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of

change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose

Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. The proposed approach, which leverages numerical optimization techniques and the PyROA algorithm, successfully generates customized code patterns for various compressed sensing schemes, resulting in significantly improved reconstruction quality in comparison to random code patterns, as demonstrated by experimental results. The research's contributions are particularly relevant to the fields of compressed sensing, signal processing, and imaging technology. The developed approach and obtained results are available within the research's repository, which can be accessed for use in related applications. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. The research found that the YORP acceleration in these asteroids varied greatly, with certain large asteroids like Geographos exhibiting a slower acceleration than expected and smaller asteroids like 1992 SK and Toro exhibiting faster accelerations. This distinction in behavior could be attributed to mass distribution or surface properties. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the YORP effect's widespread impact on the rotational states of small asteroids, and highlights the importance of observing their light curves over time to better understand this phenomenon and the conditions that influence it. Additionally, mapping the YORP acceleration in asteroids can serve as a means of classifying them based on their mass, size, and surface characteristics, and may also influence their evolution in the solar system. The research suggests that the YORP effect has the power to lead to the destruction of asteroids with extremely fast rotation rates due to their inherent instability, and could be a critical factor in shaping the distribution of rotation periods among small asteroids. The study's findings will serve as a foundation for future observations and modeling efforts. The data used in this research are archived in the Planetary Data System, and the parameter files used for modeling are available in the public repository at https://github.com/yorkopyorp. The movie files showing the shape reconstructions of the studied asteroids are available at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7mdK4cJpH6AaA0g6gM4laA. The research was conducted by combining previous observations with new photometric data

This result extends by characterization an analogous finding specific to non-positive surface genres, previously obtained by Hahn and Schreier. Additionally, our investigation leads to an extension of the standard property of topological compactness to the setting of topologies defined by invariant neighborhoods. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. Finally, some limitations are identified in the current formulation to prioritize simplicity over generality.

Moreover, this research paves the way for extending the notion of continuity to a wider range of functions that are considered important in string transducer studies.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The methods used here provide a framework for investigating the animacy spectrum across different species and in different cultures. The VTC animacy database is also presented as a publicly accessible resource. The research discussed herein is relevant to various fields including neuroscience, anthropology, psychology, and philosophy, and the findings offer implications for the development of automated detection systems for animal entities in visual scenes. The code and data associated with this study are accessible at https://github.vtc-animals. This extension facilitates a key aspect of the original proposal, namely the derivation of a predicate that indicates when two programs exhibit essentially the same behaviour, despite differing in other aspects. However, we have discovered an issue with the original proposal, specifically regarding the availability of a particular predicate, which we have found to be an instance of the problem addressed by the famous Diestel's Lemma, and thus not provable within the monadic second-order logic used in the original proposal. Nevertheless, we have successfully proved that the solvability of this instance of Diestel's Lemma is equivalent to the solvability of a particular form of Boolean formula that arises from the analysis of a type of quantum protocol known as the "Simon protocol". Furthermore, we have discovered additional connections between this formula and other related concepts, including the complexity class called the "complementary Simon problem" and a quantum circuit known as the "Fourier transform circuit". Finally, we have provided an illustration of the practical applications of this new logic by incorporating "expectations' through an example related to the "Simon protocol'. This example also demonstrates the potential advantages of using the quantum Hoare logic to analyze the properties of quantum programs when compared to other approaches, particularly in terms of the level of detail provided and the ease of use. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. The proposed correction technique is available for the community to use, and further optimization strategies are suggested for future development, including integrating inversion codes and data pre-processing pipelines into single, integrated frameworks. The current study contributes to the understanding and management of Bperp bias, as well as the development of techniques for improving accuracy in vector magnetic field mappings. The most promising approach involves fitting the fill fraction explicitly, along with other factors like noise and field strength. The research provides actionable advice for users, offer the source code for the correction technique openly, and recommends best practices for optimizing inversion algorithms and data combinations. The study's objectives, approach, and findings are relevant to vector magnetic field analysis in general, and its methods can be applied to other observed data sets. The paper's results highlight the importance of accurately resolving 180deg ambiguity in Bperp, emphasizing that the minimum allowable noise standard for global-scale observations should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the relevant spatial scales and associated structures. The most critical recommendation from this study is that data sets with large bias in Bperp, particularly the perpendicular component, especially those involving global-scale structures, should be treated with caution and possibly replaced with empirically-derived model boundaries

Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our demonstration includes a solid state physics example - the Heisenberg spin chain - as well as a non-condensed phase Monte Carlo simulation of a complex-valued field theory. These examples showcase the feasibility of computing relevant physical quantities with precise accuracy. Our design's scalability is compatible with upcoming large-scale computational capabilities. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To this end, we propose a novel approach called Neural Network Loss Explorer (NLLSE), an iterative procedure that determines the optimal loss function by dynamically updating it during network training. NLLSE identifies the loss function parameters that maximize performance on a validation set, using cross-validation to ensure robustness and hyperparameter efficacy testing to determine suitability across different datasets. Our experiments demonstrate NLLSE's capabilities on datasets representing real-world applications, showing that it is possible to improve performance by using a learning approach to loss function selection. Our approach, NLLSE, offers a distinctive contribution by treating the loss function as a parameter that can be refined during training, going beyond the conventional, static loss function choices that have long characterized deep learning methodologies. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. NISQ-HHL's compact design allows for seamless integration with existing hybrid HHL frameworks, thereby facilitating the seamless transition to Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware for a wide range of applications. Experimental outcomes on real hardware demonstrate NISQ-HHL's efficiency, showing that QCRLL2, a challenging noisy-qubit circuit, is feasible on the Quantinuum System Model H1-1 following hybrid initialization of all qubits. Moreover, NISQ-HHL's performance is compared to state-of-the-art hybrid HHL variations, demonstrating its superior execution times for real-world portfolio-optimization tasks on up-to-date noisy-qubit hardware. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This confirms the effectiveness of the proposed attention mechanism in efficient ASR using multi-modal learning. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In order to facilitate integration with existing research on this topic, we also present results in a format compatible with existing 'well mixed' models, revealing that the error in underestimating transmission risk can be substantial, with estimates suggesting that up to twenty-fold more aerosol particles may remain in the air than previously assumed, depending on specific conditions. Consequently, we propose that a more accurate'minimum mixing' model is necessary to adequately capture the complexity of aerosol transport in enclosed spaces. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the dynamics influencing the behavior of aerosols in confined environments is crucial for developing effective strategies to prevent the spread of airborne transmitted diseases. Until now, this understanding has been limited by the availability of numerical data. By making our complete dataset publicly accessible, we intend to facilitate further research on this critical topic. Specifically, our data package includes detailed visualizations, raw numerical data, model source code, and comprehensive guidelines for its use, with the aim of contributing to ongoing efforts to model the transport and transmission of airborne pathogens. To this end, we also outline anticipated research directions that our data package enables, such as the exploration of similar problems in other enclosed settings, the investigation of surface deposition of aerosols, and the analysis of different ventilation methods. Moreover, we anticipate that our findings will be relevant to policy-makers and bus operators, who can use the results to inform decisions about safety protocols and ventilation strategies in urban buses. Finally, we emphasize that the spread of airborne transmitted diseases in confined environments is a complex issue that affects us all, and we must continue to refine our understanding of it through further research. By doing so, we can better protect ourselves and others from this ongoing global health challenge. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, a model based on the elastic scattering hypothesis successfully explains the magnetic anisotropy and Hall effect behaviors. Although the Anomotous Anisotropy of Resistivity in the most slender layers can be attributed to the Rashba effect, a comparison with theoretical predictions indicates that the spin-orbit proximity effect's magnitude may be insufficient to realize the self-consistent enhancement of Zero-Bias Spin-Orbit Coupling for topological quantum phases. Nonetheless, this research demonstrates that spin-orbit proximity coupling can substantially influence the magnetic transport properties of Bismuth-enriched layers, offering a promising avenue for exploring novel magnetic quantum phases at the interface of nonmagnetic and ferromagnetic layers. A discussion on the relevant science and technology, including grapheneenriched layers, is also presented in this work. Finally, an examination of the multilayer technique's limitations is presented, along with proposals for addressing these constraints, such as using Antimony instead of Bismuth. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We hope that the methodology and findings presented can serve as a foundation for future work involving the training of neural networks with specified performance guarantees. The code we used is now openly available. The significance of ensuring a neural network's sensitivity to input is explored in applications such as classification systems that are transparent and secure, and in systems that combine machine learning with optimisation to ensure a neural network does not over-generalise. We also investigated the relationship between input sensitivity and a neural network's ability to identify patterns, finding that restricting the network's sensitivity can prevent it from learning to some extent, although the extent of this prevention varies greatly depending on the data in question. The method we developed to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant also provides the basis for calculating another key measure of input sensitivity, known as the neural network's total variation. We thus have a way to differentiate between the network's ability to identify patterns and its sensitivity to input, and have made the code we used in this research openly available. This code enables other researchers to utilize the method we developed to determine the upper and lower bounds for a neural network's total variation and Lipschitz constants, and to test the approach we used themselves. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Despite being specifically designed for ditau events, this code can also be used to simulate other processes involving the production of heavy vector leptoquarks. For instance, it can be utilized to analyze events characterized by the decay of vector leptoquarks into a Z boson and a tau lepton, as well as those defined by the decay of vector leptoquarks into a W boson and a bottom quark. For reference, the code predicts the correct number of events for ditau production at the LHC with its full configuration, consisting of a 13 TeV energy and an integrated luminosity of 137 inverse picobarns. This predicts the following: a predicted range of (3.58, 3.71) inverse barns for the phrase "produce 1 event of ditau" at the 97% confidence level. This code can be obtained from the website of the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). The name of the code is "DilepQ at NLO" and it is compatible with versions 3 and higher of the Monte Carlo event generator code "MadGraph". To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The most effective model obtained displayed a 307% improvement in precision when compared to the traditional Euclidean approach, thus providing a viable solution for a wide range of indoor location estimation applications. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In the process, this research also clarifies the relationship between beam breakup threshold current, filling pattern, and machine design, providing a theoretical framework for further research into this complex subject. Ultimately, it is demonstrated that filling patterns affecting beam breakup can be influenced by changing machine design parameters, availing opportunities to optimize design for minimized instability effects. A case study involving a 1.8 GeV energy recovery linac illustrates the practical value of this research, showcasing how filling patterns can be optimized to alleviate beam breakup limitations and boost design performance. Furthermore, this study paves the ground for the investigation of other energy recovery linacs, highlighting the widespread impact of filling patterns on beam breakup and suggesting that a significant portion of currently inoperable or poorly utilized energy recovery linacs could be revived with the help of advanced filling patterns. In addition, it is emphasized that the energy recovery linac discussed in the paper case study is already in operation, allowing for the value of optimized design to be measured directly and highlighting the substantial practical benefits of this research. Finally, it is pointed out that the term beam breakup threshold current is sometimes defined differently by various researchers, leading to potential confusion, and to clarify this issue, a new standard definition of beam breakup threshold current is proposed. It is also pointed out that research on beam breakup often focuses on causes, effects, and prevention methods but tends to overlook the key factor of filling patterns that influence the stability of energy recovery linacs. It is further observed that filling patterns can affect not only beam breakup but also the performance of energy recovery linacs in general, allowing for the exploration of new opportunities for optimizing their design, and that this research is intended to contribute to this under-explored area of study. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Furthermore, this study provides a useful framework for incorporating curved brush geometries into coexistence curve calculations, phase field models, and other multi-scale simulations. Our results are essential for the development of curved substrate models and have significant implications for the understanding of nanoscale dimensions and free energy of block copolymer melts. Additionally, we reveal how the introduction of solvent affects the size of the end exclusion zone and chain polarization in good solvents, offering a novel perspective on solvent-induced brush swelling. This knowledge can be utilized to develop a revised solvent-induced brush swelling model. We also discover that the distinction between weak and strong stretching brush geometry diminishes with increasing Gaussian curvature, revealing an intriguing 'concave universe' where the rules of weak stretching brushes emerge on tiny, curved regions of strong stretching brushes. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the 'end exclusion zone' concept is a fundamental property of curved, stretched brushes that arises from the intrinsic geometry of the surface and the attached polymer chains, completely independent of the enthalpic chain-solvent interaction. Consequently, this unique understanding will likely lead to the development of novel nanoscale materials and architectures inspired by the intricate geometry of curved polymer brushes.
