A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. Our analysis of its parameters through the Markov chain Monte Carlo method reveals that it meets all the constraints derived from the observed rates of the universe's expansion, the matter density, the temperature, and the anisotropy of the cosmic background radiation. Our research concludes that this model exhibits a high degree of robustness across various observations and constraints. It is noteworthy that this model's simplicity contrasts with the complexity of its results. Our computation of the future universe's evolution reveals that this model predicts a steady transition to a dark energy-dominated phase, which will result in the universe's continued expansion. Our estimation of the model's parameters through the Markov chain Monte Carlo method further reveal that the model's current deceleration, density, and effective equation of state parameter are 0.038, 8.848 × 10^-27 kg/m^3, and -0.038 respectively. Our study of the model's future evolution reveals a deceleration parameter of -1.0 and a density of 10.0 × 10^-27 kg/m^3. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Our research demonstrates that J/ψ invisible decays offer a promising connection between particle and nuclear physics, and dark matter physics, with potential for significant progress in the near future. Our study also emphasizes the importance of considering the production and decay of J/ψ in a unified analysis to ensure accuracy in understanding J/ψ effective interactions. Furthermore, our research indicates that J/ψ effective interactions can be sensitive to certain types of new physics such as light sterile neutrinos and certain dark matter scenarios, with potential for discovery in near-future experiments. Our research code is available at https://github.com/HuangHuaSheng/JPsiInvisibleDecay. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A demonstration of GCNN's versatility shows that it can be applied to existing CNN structures to empower them with the ability to handle imprecise inputs, thereby solidifying the foundation of GCNNs within the broader Neural Network community. In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then described as non-flat connections, from which conserved charges can be deduced using established formulas, albeit those of standard Chern-Simons theory. The soliton's stability and characteristics are determined based on holonomic constraints along cyclic paths, while in rotating hairy black holes cases, the theory allows recovery of the temperature and chemical potential. The entropy generated by the black holes in these scenarios remains consistent with that predicted by the Chern-Simons theory. The conformal equivalent to this framework describes General Relativity's interaction with a cosmologically constant scalar field. The redefinition of the Chern-Simons form for this system, using suitable composite gauge fields, is explored in a simplified form. The paper also presents an interpretation of the scalar field's self-interaction as a result of the Chern-Simons form's non-linear characteristics. The self-interaction's strength can be controlled through the use of an auxiliary parameter, which affects the curvature of the Chern-Simons form. The curvature's relationship to the cosmological constant also means that the latter can be defined in a way that is independent of the curvature of the spacetime. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our approach is called separate-but-shared (SBS) dynamics model, and
our results demonstrate that it efficiently extracts task-specific information
from the shared structure without being hindered by the natural difficulty of
learning multiple, unrelated dynamics. Our code is available at https://github.com/hughishere/sbs_dynamics. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, because GANs tend to be noisy and dependent on specific training data, we regularized the model to reduce this dependence and ensure the generated samples align with the underlying prior distribution. This prior regularization also enabled the model to handle various prior distributions seamlessly, simply by incorporating the prior into the energy function used in training, which simplifies the model's implementation and enables the generation of non-negative images efficiently. We demonstrated the effectiveness and flexibility of this model by applying it to multiple inverse problems and complex datasets. The code for this project has been made public and is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yangyi1993/WASPGAN. Furthermore, we provided comparative analyses with current state-of-the-art methods and implemented the model on a variety of datasets and problems to ensure its scalability and versatility. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's small size, 0.54 parsecs in diameter, suggests it is likely caused by a cloud of dense plasma that lies along the line of sight to the pulsar, partially blocking its sightline and influencing its scintillation patterns over decades. The paper further explores the relationship between this screen and the surrounding bubble structure, the necessary mass of the screen to maintain its stability, and the potential consequences of COVID-19-like space phenomena for the pulsar. Additionally, a preliminary estimate of the screen's density is provided. The techniques employed in this study demonstrate how extensive pulsar scintillation observations can be used to map the interstellar medium with high spatial and temporal resolution. The level of detail achieved in this analysis highlights the potential for a dedicated survey that through extensive pulsar scintillation observations can map the interstellar medium with high spatial and temporal resolution, potentially revealing screens similar to the one analyzed here on a larger scale, and providing a comprehensive understanding of the medium's dynamic structures. The paper's findings also suggest that such a survey could facilitate the detection of screens associated with voids in the interstellar medium, which could, in turn, reveal the screens' effects on the surrounding gas, specifically in the Local Bubble region. The interaction between the screens and the surrounding gas could result from COVID-19-like space phenomena causing mass loss in the voids, and may have implications for the pulsars located within them. The paper concludes with a proposal for a dedicated survey that can map the interstellar medium through extensive pulsar scintillation observations, and explores the potential for such a survey to detect screens associated with voids in the interstellar medium.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, QPNet is applied to unsupervised songbird birdcase (BS) waveform generation using only recorded songs, showing that it can successfully reconstruct unseen parts of learned spectra. The generated waveform maintaining the same periodicity and fidelity as actual birdcase songs, surpasses the baseline WN model in terms of mean squared error. The proposed QPNet framework provides a versatile model suitable for various quasi-periodic signal generation tasks. The code for QPNet is available at https://github.com/Cheng-Lin-Hsiao/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. The effectiveness of QPNet in audio waveform generation is demonstrated in accompanying animation videos on YouTube at https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLQ6EH6Y3J1b3Q6Q1Q8. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our sound source localization algorithm has been open-sourced on GitHub, along with VGG-Sound Source which can be accessed through the project website.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN achieves comparable performance to GCNs in Euclidean geometry on small, less distorted graphs. The LGCN code is available at https://github.com/XiaofengNiu/LGCN. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our exponential model can be applied to value
learning through a process similar to the value-based learning theory proposed by
Rachlin, using updates of the discount factor. Through value learning, our model
can be tested for factorization, which has implications for understanding the
automatic nature of value learning. Additionally, we discuss the potential for
our model to explain psychological phenomena such as loss aversion and the
endowment effect. Finally, we propose a new method for estimating the
distribution of delay discounting parameters, which offers greater precision than
existing methods while minimizing the loss of statistical power. This new
methodology can be utilized for future delay discounting research. We also
investigate the delay discounting preferences of a sample of students through
actual economic decisions, using an incentive-compatible task designed to
minimize strategic behavior. Our findings confirm the expected relationships
between delay discounting and variables such as age, income, and education, as
well as the internal consistency of the Tsallis distribution. Most notably, our
data reveal a distinct dual nature of delay discounting impulsivity, with
impulsivity varying significantly between different types of delays. We
hypothetically apply our model to a policy scenario involving a one-time
transfer payment, and find that the standard exponential model overestimates
the discount rate when delay discounting variability is not considered. Our
model also predicts that the dual nature of delay discounting impulsivity will
lead to a one-time transfer payment being split between immediate consumption
and future savings, with the latter being saved for a period of time before
being consumed. We refer to this behavior as the 'delayed consumption effect'. We
also observe this delayed consumption effect in our sample of students, where
the median delay is approximately 7 months. We propose policy interventions

Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. Furthermore, the canonical thermal equilibrium state is found to correspond to a loxodromic dynamics, whereas both the semiclassical and high-temperature approximations result in parabolic dynamics. Nonetheless, despite the complexity of the associated metaplectic operator, the canonical thermal equilibrium state can be explicitly reconstructed from the Weyl-Wigner symbols. Ultimately, this analysis reveals the underlying classical dynamics that define the thermal quantum states and demonstrate that the loxodromic dynamics are the sole candidate fulfilling the requirements of being both symplectically invariant and explicitly observable. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we highlight the implications of negative absolute temperature on the entropy of a two-level system and demonstrate its relationship with the Boltzmann distribution. Lastly, we examine the applicability of these concepts to quantum mechanics. Despite the fact that negative absolute temperature was initially proposed by Denkman and Raymer in 1975, it remains a topic of ongoing research, with a notable example being the study on trapped ions presented in the paper by Daems and Braun in 2011. This research has also been related to negative absolute temperature in the studies conducted on bosonic atoms and optical systems. Notably, the idea has been applied in the development of negative absolute temperature sensors. With all these advancements, the significance of negative absolute temperature in the field continues to grow, offering numerous possibilities for future research. This report is an adaptation of the presentation given at the International Conference on Statistical Mechanics, held in Puebla, Mexico in 2019. This conference marked the 50th anniversary of the introduction of the concept of negative absolute temperature by Denkman and Raymer in 1969. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, the small branching ratio in certain $f$ electron compounds may need reevaluation in light of $d$ orbital mixing. Furthermore, our results suggest that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be a major driver of non-trivial spin-orbit coupled interactions in these materials. We highlight promising research avenues and illustrate that many aspects remain to be explored, such as $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in lower symmetry geometries and its impact on the electronic and magnetic properties of realistic material structures. In the process, we offer a detailed analysis of the relevant materials science and physics, incorporating examples from 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, as well as d and f electron compounds. In the appendices, we provide additional technical information on the methods used, including the spin-orbital Hamiltonian parameterization and the generation of $d$-shell configurations. Additionally, we present theoretical magnetic property calculations for all possible $d$-shell configurations in a cubic crystal structure. Moreover, we discuss the relationship between the spin-orbital Hamiltonian and the Weyl vector of the Landau-Lifshitz energy functional. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Moreover, it highlights the potential applications of these findings in predicting quantum coefficients. Lastly, it introduces the concept of genus-zero decay, which can be used to extend the predictions about quantum coefficients to a broader range of values. This achievement is made possible by combining the results presented in this research with the insights gained from the mathematical properties of string theory and its connections to the geometry of the related moduli spaces. This knowledge enables the conversion of mathematical representations into predictive models of Coates and Getzler, which in turn facilitate the expansion of the quantum coefficients beyond the genus-zero decay threshold. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our research, a beginning step in medical GAN usage, presents a starting point for multiple interesting scenarios, such as creating realistic synthetic medical images, improving existing classification models through data augmentation, and developing explanations for deep learning models through feature importance analysis. numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
